questions.question: Where two driving lanes merge into one, what does the zipper merge method require?
options: Cars from both lanes take turns entering the single lane
Cars already in the continuing lane always go first
Cars in the lane that ends must wait for a full gap
Cars must merge well before the lanes actually narrow
questions.explanation: Alternating one car from each lane, like the teeth of a zipper, keeps both queues moving and is the recommended conduct at obstacles and at the end of acceleration lanes.

questions.question: How should you meet an oncoming vehicle on a narrow gravel road?
options: Keep your speed and move slightly towards the right
Stay in the middle where the surface is most firm
Reduce speed well in advance and move far to the right
Stop completely and wait until the other car has passed
questions.explanation: A large part of the Icelandic road network is gravel, and a timely, significant reduction in speed plus a position far right is what prevents loose stones and off-road wheels from causing a loss of control.

questions.question: An oncoming car is driving straight towards you on your side of the road. What is the correct action?
options: Move over into the left lane that the other car has left
Hold your lane and flash your headlights until it moves
Accelerate so you clear the stretch before it reaches you
Reduce speed, move far right, and stop if necessary
questions.explanation: Drivers on the wrong side usually notice at the last moment and swerve back to their own side, so moving left would put you straight back in their path; signalling with headlights or the horn is an addition, not a substitute.

questions.question: Overtaking must normally be done on the left. What is the single exception?
options: The vehicle ahead is driving below the speed limit
The vehicle ahead is clearly about to turn left
The vehicle ahead has signalled you to come past
The road has two marked lanes in your direction
questions.explanation: A vehicle that is turning left vacates the right-hand part of the carriageway, so passing it on the right is the only situation the book allows for right-sided overtaking.

questions.question: According to the main principle, when may you overtake at a road junction?
options: Only when you are travelling on the road that has priority
Only when the junction carries no give way or stop sign
Only with full visibility and certainty that there is no danger
Only when the vehicle ahead is signalling a right turn
questions.explanation: Junctions add vehicles entering and leaving the road plus the risk that the car ahead turns left, so the book demands absolute visibility before any overtaking there.

questions.question: The driver ahead switches on the right indicator to tell you the road is clear to pass. How should you treat that signal?
options: As a reliable confirmation that the road is clear
As a courtesy that must not be trusted blindly
As an instruction that you are obliged to overtake
As a warning that the driver is about to turn right
questions.explanation: Responsibility for the manoeuvre stays entirely with the overtaking driver, who must judge the road himself; the other driver may have misjudged or may mean something else.

questions.question: A line of cars has built up behind a slow vehicle. Which driver should overtake first?
options: The driver at the very back of the line of cars
The driver whose vehicle has the strongest engine
The driver immediately behind the slow vehicle
Whichever driver first finds a suitable gap ahead
questions.explanation: Passing in order keeps the manoeuvre predictable; if that driver does not want to overtake he must leave a gap so the next one can pass the cars one step at a time.

questions.question: How accurately can a driver judge the speed of a car about 300 metres away?
options: It is practically impossible to tell 30 km/h from 70 km/h
Only speeds above roughly 90 km/h are hard to estimate
An experienced driver can estimate it within 5 km/h
Speeds can be judged reliably out to about 500 metres
questions.explanation: An oncoming vehicle barely changes in apparent size at that range, which is why head-on collisions during overtaking are so often serious.

questions.question: Why must you leave plenty of space when overtaking a cyclist?
options: Gravel thrown up by your tyres can strike the rider
The rider may swerve to avoid a pothole you cannot see
A cyclist must by law be given the whole driving lane
The draft behind your car can throw the rider off balance
questions.explanation: A passing vehicle drags a strong gust of air in its wake, and the effect grows with both the size of the vehicle and its speed.

questions.question: When may a driver make a U-turn or reverse on a road?
options: Only where the posted speed limit is 50 km/h or lower
Only on roads with a single driving lane in each direction
Only when it causes no danger or inconvenience to others
Only when no other vehicle is within about 100 metres
questions.explanation: The permission depends on the circumstances rather than on a fixed limit, and it is usually safer to drive on and turn around somewhere off the road.

questions.question: How should you control your speed when reversing down a slope?
options: By adjusting the pressure on the clutch pedal
By pulling the handbrake in short, light pulls
By adjusting the pressure on the brake pedal
By selecting a lower gear before you set off
questions.explanation: On level ground the clutch can meter the speed, but on a decline gravity is driving the car, so only the brake keeps it slow.

questions.question: Two lanes narrow so that cars cannot pass side by side, and one car is clearly further ahead. Who has the right of way?
options: The car in the lane that continues
The car that is further forward
The car that is on the right-hand side
The car that arrived at higher speed
questions.explanation: The car behind slows and stops if needed; the right-hand car only gains priority in the different case where the two vehicles are level with each other.

questions.question: What is the maximum permitted speed in a pedestrianized residential street?
options: 15 km/h
10 km/h
20 km/h
30 km/h
questions.explanation: These streets are shared by vehicles and pedestrians alike, and drivers must additionally give way to people on foot.

questions.question: How is the three-second rule used to set your gap to the car ahead?
options: Do not reach a fixed object until three seconds after the car ahead
Stay at least three car lengths behind the vehicle in front
Be able to brake your car to a standstill within three seconds
Wait three seconds after the car in front touches its brakes
questions.explanation: Timing a lamp post or sign gives a gap that scales automatically with speed; the counting phrase "one one-thousand, two one-thousand, three one-thousand" approximates the interval.

questions.question: The stopping distance of a vehicle is made up of which two parts?
options: The braking distance and an extra safety margin
The reaction distance and the braking distance
The reaction distance and the following distance
The braking distance and the skidding distance
questions.explanation: The car keeps travelling while the driver perceives the hazard and moves to the pedal, and only then does the braking begin; the sum of the two is the stopping distance.

questions.question: Which of these makes a driver's reaction distance longer?
options: Driving on gravel instead of dry asphalt
Talking on a mobile phone while driving
Having worn tyres with very little tread
Braking while heading down a steep slope
questions.explanation: Reaction distance depends on speed and on the driver's alertness, so fatigue, intoxication, phone use and distraction lengthen it; the other three affect the braking distance instead.

questions.question: If the speed of a car is doubled, what happens to its braking distance?
options: It becomes roughly twice as long
It becomes roughly three times as long
It becomes roughly eight times as long
It becomes roughly four times as long
questions.explanation: Braking distance follows the kinetic energy of the car, which rises with the square of the speed: double the speed and the braking distance is roughly four times as long.

questions.question: What is the basic requirement that visibility places on your choice of speed?
options: You must be able to stop within twice the road you can see
You must be able to stop within three seconds of a hazard
You must keep the posted limit whatever the visibility
You must be able to stop within the road you can see
questions.explanation: Controlling speed this way leaves room to stop for an unseen obstacle or for another driver who ignores a give way sign or a dangerous curve.

questions.question: In which of these situations does the book say a driver may drive faster?
options: On a broad, dry asphalt road with light traffic
On a narrow, crooked road in fine, dry weather
In a residential area where children may be about
While towing a heavy trailer on a level main road
questions.explanation: Speed must be chosen from the road, the visibility, the traffic, the vehicle and the driver together, and only a wide dry road with little traffic relaxes all of them at once.
